Explain the need for FragmentTransactions
cards.backText:
A FragmentTransaction groups changes to fragments managed by a FragmentManager. Use it to add, replace, remove, show, or hide fragments, then commit the changes.

FragmentManager manager = getSupportFragmentManager();
FragmentTransaction transaction = manager.beginTransaction();
transaction.replace(R.id.detailsContainer, new DetailsFragment());
transaction.addToBackStack(null);
transaction.commit();

The container must exist in the Activity’s layout. addToBackStack makes this change reversible through the fragment back stack; it is optional when that navigation behavior is not wanted. commit() submits the changes; creating a transaction alone does not display the replacement.

Slides: 12, pp. 13–20, 54, 68. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
7. Fragments

Describe the difference between ListView and ListFragment
cards.backText:
ListView is a View/widget that displays a scrolling list. It needs an adapter to supply its rows.

ListFragment is a specialized Fragment that provides a list-based UI around a ListView. It has a Fragment lifecycle and offers convenience methods such as setListAdapter and getListView, plus the onListItemClick callback.

@Override
public void onListItemClick(ListView list, View view,
                            int position, long id) {
    showDetails(position);
}

This method goes in a ListFragment subclass; showDetails is an application-defined helper. A custom ListFragment layout uses the expected @android:id/list identifier for its ListView. The widget and the Fragment hosting it are different types of objects.

Slides: 11, pp. 82–86; 12, pp. 40, 52–56. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Carefully review chapter 10 and lecture slides on eLC
cards.backText:
• Use Lecture 13, IntroToNavPatterns: it covers the navigational patterns listed in this review section.
  • Navigation relationships: lateral, descendant, Back, and ancestral/Up navigation (pp. 14–24), with targets and click-handler code (pp. 30–32).
  • Navigation UI: swipe views, tabs, drawers, and master/detail flow (pp. 33–45); action bars, menus, action buttons, and FABs (pp. 48–69).
  • Single activity: one hosting Activity with different Fragments for different screens (pp. 46–47, 72–73).
  • Dialogs: their purpose, DialogFragment, creation, showing, dismissal, and examples (pp. 76–105).

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 14–105. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Distinguish between back and up navigation
cards.backText:
• Back follows the back stack: the default behavior returns to the last Activity or Fragment placed on the stack. Activities are managed in last-in, first-out order; Back removes the most recently added Activity.
  • Up follows the screen hierarchy: ancestral navigation moves to a screen’s logical ancestor/parent. It is useful when the app has more than one hierarchy level.
  • Why they can differ: Back depends on the visited screen history; Up depends on the declared parent relationship. A previous sibling screen need not be the current screen’s parent.
  • Activities and Up: declare android:parentActivityName in the descendant Activity’s manifest entry and enable the action bar’s Up affordance with setDisplayHomeAsUpEnabled(true). A theme displaying the action bar is needed to see it.
  • Fragments and Back: use addToBackStack() when you want a fragment change to be reversible by Back.

Up navigation setup

<activity
    android:name=".FirstChildActivity"
    android:parentActivityName=".SimpleParentChildSiblingActivity" />
// Inside onCreate(), after obtaining the Activity's ActionBar:
myActionBar.setDisplayHomeAsUpEnabled(true);

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 21–29. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Be able to understand and describe these basic navigational patterns:

  • Target navigation (lateral, descendant, ancestral)
  • Swipe views
  • Tabs
  • Navigation drawer
  • Master/detail flow
  • Action bar, menus, and action buttons
  • Floating Action Button
  • Dialogs
cards.backText:
• Target navigation: a clickable target, such as a button, opens a destination. Lateral moves between sibling destinations on the same hierarchy level; descendant goes deeper; ancestral/Up goes to an ancestor.
  • Swipe views: gesture-based movement between pages. The slides show image pages and use androidx.viewpager2.widget.ViewPager2; ViewPager2 supersedes ViewPager and supports vertical paging.
  • Tabs: visible tab choices select pages, as in the Image 1 / Image 2 / Image 3 example. The updated class is com.google.android.material.tabs.TabLayout.
  • Navigation drawer: a navigation panel containing destination choices. The slide shows Email, Info, and Map. Use AndroidX DrawerLayout with a Material NavigationView supplying the header and menu.
  • Master/detail flow: a list/grid Fragment selects an item whose details appear in another Fragment. Single-pane: launch an Activity for details. Double-pane: display both Fragments side by side.
  • Action bar, menus, and action buttons: expose the Activity’s actions. Buttons can be icons, text, or both; actions that do not fit go into overflow. The slides name options, context, and pop-up menus.
  • Floating Action Button: exposes the primary action, such as adding a contact. The updated class is Material FloatingActionButton.
  • Dialogs: present a focused acknowledgment, confirmation, or small task. The slides recommend managing a dialog with AndroidX DialogFragment.

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 14–24, 30–69, 76–105. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Target navigation (lateral, descendant, ancestral)
cards.backText:
• Target: a visible control initiates navigation. In the professor’s example, buttons open child screens or sibling screens; a click listener constructs an Intent and calls startActivity().
  • Lateral: move between screens on the same hierarchy level. Swipe navigation, tabs, or other controls can support this. For sibling Activities below the top level, declare the same parentActivityName for each.
  • Descendant: move deeper into the hierarchy, from an ancestor screen to a child screen. Declare the child’s parent in the manifest, create an Intent for the child, and call startActivity().
  • Ancestral/Up: move upward to the ancestor. Set the descendant’s correct manifest parent and enable the action bar’s Up affordance with setDisplayHomeAsUpEnabled(true).
  • Classify the relationship: sibling → sibling is lateral; parent → child is descendant; child → parent is ancestral.

A navigation target from the slides

Button firstChild = findViewById(R.id.firstChild);
firstChild.setOnClickListener(new View.OnClickListener() {
    @Override
    public void onClick(View v) {
        Intent intent = new Intent(getApplicationContext(),
                                   FirstChildActivity.class);
        startActivity(intent);
    }
});

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 14–24, 30–32. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Swipe views
cards.backText:
• Purpose: let the user navigate between pages by swiping. The slide illustration shows image pages moving across the display.
  • Lateral navigation: swipe views can connect screens/pages residing on the same hierarchy level; tabs can also be used alongside this navigation.
  • Use ViewPager2: androidx.viewpager2.widget.ViewPager2 supersedes ViewPager and also supports vertical paging. The lecture shows pages with an ImageView and TextView.
  • Size in the slide example: width and height are 0dp with constraints to all four parent edges, so the pager fills the constrained area.
  • Back-stack design: do not automatically put dozens or hundreds of paged Fragments on the back stack just to reach an ancestor. The slides warn that this could force a user to press Back through every page; ancestral navigation addresses the return to the ancestor.

ViewPager2 inside a ConstraintLayout

<androidx.viewpager2.widget.ViewPager2
    android:id="@+id/viewpager"
    android:layout_width="0dp"
    android:layout_height="0dp"
    app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
    app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent" />

The enclosing ConstraintLayout declares the android and app XML namespaces.

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 14, 33–37. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Tabs
cards.backText:
• Purpose: provide visible choices for switching between pages. The slide’s example has Image 1, Image 2, and Image 3 tabs, with the selected page indicated.
  • Navigation relationship: tabs are one way to support lateral navigation across screens on the same hierarchy level. They can be used with swipe navigation.
  • Updated class: use com.google.android.material.tabs.TabLayout rather than the older support-design TabLayout shown in the textbook example.
  • Pager connection: the slides mention FragmentPagerAdapter and FragmentStateAdapter; the latter is used with ViewPager2.

A TabLayout in an XML layout

<com.google.android.material.tabs.TabLayout
    android:id="@+id/tab_layout"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content" />

This declares the tab control. The page/tab content still has to be supplied; the tag alone does not create three image pages.

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 14, 38–39. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Navigation drawer
cards.backText:
• Purpose: offer a navigation panel with destination choices. The professor’s screenshot shows a drawer listing Email, Info, and Map.
  • Container: the updated class is androidx.drawerlayout.widget.DrawerLayout, replacing the older support-library version.
  • Navigation contents: place a Material com.google.android.material.navigation.NavigationView alongside the main app content inside DrawerLayout.
  • Principal attributes in the slide: android:layout_gravity="start" places the drawer at the start side; app:headerLayout supplies its header layout; app:menu supplies its menu items.

Drawer structure from the slide example

<androidx.drawerlayout.widget.DrawerLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
    android:id="@+id/drawer_layout"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent">

    <!-- Main app content goes here. -->

    <com.google.android.material.navigation.NavigationView
        android:id="@+id/nvView"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="match_parent"
        android:layout_gravity="start"
        android:background="@android:color/white"
        app:headerLayout="@layout/nav_header"
        app:menu="@menu/jobleads_menu" />
</androidx.drawerlayout.widget.DrawerLayout>

The referenced header and menu resources define what the drawer displays; handling a selected destination is app-dependent.

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 40–42. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Master detail flow
cards.backText:
• Master: a list or grid of items, supplied by one Fragment.
  • Detail: the associated information for the selected item, supplied by another Fragment.
  • Single-pane layout: selecting an item launches a new Activity that displays the detail Fragment. The slides show a topic list followed by a Topic Detail screen.
  • Double-pane layout: show the master and detail Fragments side by side. The lecture’s wider-screen example uses available width of 600dp; the arrangement can also be affected by orientation.
  • Reuse: the list/detail pieces can serve both arrangements instead of duplicating their behavior.
  • Selected state: the earlier AndroidVersionsFragments example saves the selected list index and restores the appropriate detail after rotation.

Slides: 13, IntroToNavPatterns, PDF pp. 43–45. Related professor example: Lecture 12, pp. 24–39, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code fragments are practice adaptations of the professor’s examples; named Activities, views, and resources must exist in the app.

cards.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Action bar, Menus, and Action Buttons
cards.backText:
• ActionBar: presents actions available to an Activity; actions can be added or removed from an Activity or Fragment. The lecture names androidx.appcompat.app.ActionBar.
  • Navigation and controls: the bar can expose Up navigation, search, tabs, or a drop-down control. The slides show an Up arrow next to Topic Detail.
  • Menus: the three menu types named in the lecture are options, context, and pop-up menus.
  • Action buttons: icons, text, or both that represent commands. The slide example shows Add and Close on the bar, with Help in the overflow menu.
  • Overflow: holds actions that do not fit on the main action bar. Order items by importance/frequency using android:orderInCategory.
  • Menu XML: each <item> can specify android:id, android:icon, android:title, android:orderInCategory, and android:showAsAction.
  • showAsAction values in the slides: ifRoom displays the action when space permits; withText includes its title text; never places it in overflow; the slides say to avoid always when possible.
  • Callbacks: onCreateOptionsMenu() inflates the menu; onOptionsItemSelected() identifies the selected item and performs its action.
  • Toolbar: androidx.appcompat.widget.Toolbar is a generalization of ActionBar. It can replace the Activity’s action bar via setSupportActionBar(toolbar) and can also be placed elsewhere in a layout.

Menu resource and callbacks

<!-- res/menu/simple_action_menu.xml -->
<menu xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <item
        android:id="@+id/menu_add"
        android:icon="@android:drawable/ic_menu_add"
        android:orderInCategory="2"
        android:showAsAction="ifRoom|withText"
        android:title="Add" />
    <item
        android:id="@+id/menu_help"
        android:orderInCategory="5"
        android:showAsAction="never"
        android:title="Help" />
</menu>
@Override
public boolean onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu menu) {
    getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu.simple_action_menu, menu);
    return true;
}

@Override
public boolean onOptionsItemSelected(MenuItem item) {
    if (item.getItemId() == R.id.menu_add) {
        Toast.makeText(this, "Add Clicked", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show();
        return true;
    }
    return super.onOptionsItemSelected(item);
}

Floating Action Button
cards.backText:
• Purpose: perform the primary action of a particular Activity.
  • Professor’s example: a contacts app uses the FAB to initiate adding a new contact by launching an Add Contact Activity. The screenshot shows a prominent floating plus button.
  • Updated class: use com.google.android.material.floatingactionbutton.FloatingActionButton instead of the older support-design class.
  • Attributes shown in the lecture: android:src chooses the add icon; android:contentDescription describes the button; android:clickable enables clicking; android:elevation supplies elevation; margins leave space from the parent’s edges.

FAB in the slide’s RelativeLayout arrangement

<com.google.android.material.floatingactionbutton.FloatingActionButton
    android:id="@+id/fab"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:layout_alignParentBottom="true"
    android:layout_alignParentEnd="true"
    android:layout_marginBottom="25dp"
    android:layout_marginEnd="25dp"
    android:clickable="true"
    android:contentDescription="Add contact"
    android:elevation="6dp"
    android:src="@android:drawable/ic_input_add" />

The placement attributes above belong to a child of RelativeLayout. A different parent uses its own placement rules. The click handler performs the app’s primary action.

Dialogs
cards.backText:
• Purpose: present a focused acknowledgment, confirmation, or small task. The slides recommend dialogs for confirming/acknowledging an action that permanently alters user data, such as deletion.
  • Editing in a dialog: offer actions to confirm or deny changes before committing them. Dialogs for simple tasks help keep the number of Activities manageable.
  • Examples: alert, progress, date-picker, time-picker, character-picker, and custom dialog windows. The lecture also lists Toast among its notification/dialog examples.
  • Recommended implementation: use androidx.fragment.app.DialogFragment. The FragmentManager manages it, and it follows nearly the same lifecycle as a Fragment.
  • Creation: override onCreateDialog(Bundle) and return the Dialog to display. An AlertDialog.Builder can supply title, message, icon, and button behavior.
  • Display and dismissal: show() displays it; dismiss() stops showing it; onDismiss() runs additional dismissal-related code.
  • AndroidX host: use a FragmentActivity (or a compatible subclass) and getSupportFragmentManager() for the AndroidX DialogFragment. Keep the support/AndroidX classes and manager consistent.
  • Custom dialogs: design a layout resource, inflate it with LayoutInflater, use it for the custom AlertDialog, and show the dialog. The same DialogFragment can also be embedded when a larger screen has room.

A compact version of the professor’s AlertDialogFragment

// Imports for the AndroidX fragment approach:
import android.app.AlertDialog;
import android.app.Dialog;
import android.os.Bundle;
import androidx.fragment.app.DialogFragment;

public class AlertDialogFragment extends DialogFragment {
    public static AlertDialogFragment newInstance() {
        return new AlertDialogFragment();
    }

    @Override
    public Dialog onCreateDialog(Bundle savedInstanceState) {
        AlertDialog.Builder builder =
            new AlertDialog.Builder(getActivity());
        builder.setTitle("Alert Dialog");
        builder.setMessage("You have been alerted.");
        builder.setPositiveButton(android.R.string.ok,
            (dialog, which) -> {
                // Perform the confirmed action here.
            });
        return builder.create();
    }
}
// Inside a FragmentActivity:
AlertDialogFragment.newInstance()
    .show(getSupportFragmentManager(), "alert");

Explain how a single activity application works
cards.backText:
• Structure: a single Activity hosts many Fragments representing different screens or parts of the app’s functionality.
  • Launch: the app starts its base/manager Activity.
  • Navigation: reuse that same Activity while changing the Fragment it hosts, rather than launching a new Activity for every screen.
  • Retained UI: portions such as the ActionBar or navigation drawer can remain as the displayed Fragment changes.
  • Advantages named in the slides: faster screen transitions, navigation managed in one place, simpler communication across screens, and a simpler AndroidManifest.

A fragment change in the existing host Activity

// Inside a FragmentActivity or compatible host:
FragmentTransaction transaction =
    getSupportFragmentManager().beginTransaction();
transaction.replace(R.id.detailsContainer, new DetailsFragment());
transaction.addToBackStack(null);
transaction.commit();

The host’s layout contains detailsContainer, and DetailsFragment supplies the destination UI. addToBackStack(null) makes this fragment change reversible with Back; it does not launch another Activity.
